new_statements.quote: An interesting dialect difference is that in Takum it is the end of a rising tone that is stressed, while in Wukari it is the beginning that is stressed. Thus forms from the two dialects which are identical in tone are quite different in stress. The phonemic status of stress, here and elsewhere, has not been completely investigated. However, there is no evidence that it is phonemic, and in at least some phrases there appears to be some freedom in the position of stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Wapan (Wukari Jukun) is a three-level tone language (high, mid, low; 1.9.1). Welmers treats stress as non-phonemic: there is no evidence of contrastive stress, and its position shows some freedom at least in some phrases; the only positional remark is phonetic and local -- on the morphologically derived rising tone glides (a dropped prefix vowel surfacing as a glide), Wukari speakers stress the beginning of the glide whereas Takum speakers stress its end. No fixed word-stress position is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author explicitly flags the phonemic status of stress as 'not completely investigated' (1949 fieldwork, three months).
new_statements.domain_note: The remark arises in the discussion of morphophonemic rising/falling tone glides at word junctures (phrase-level examples such as 'three people', 'five years'); 'here and elsewhere' extends the non-phonemic verdict to the language generally. Wukari = Wapan (wapa1235); the contrasting 'Takum' dialect is Diyi/Jukun Takum (jbu).
new_statements.identity_note: Welmers' 'Wukari' dialect is Wapan proper (speakers' self-designation /wapa/, Wukari town) = wapa1235; his contrasting 'Takum' dialect (/diyi/) is Jukun Takum, ISO jbu, Glottolog juku1254. The quoted passage compares the two; only the Wukari half applies to wapa1235. Evenhouse's ms is likewise Wapan of Wukari. The Koeln 'Phonological hierarchy' ms saved alongside is Takum (jbu), not Wapan.

sources.note: Ch. 1 Phonology; 1.9 tone: three level tonemes (high, mid, low) plus falls and a rare rise. The only stress remark is 1.9.4, p. 24 (PDF p. 31): in Wukari the beginning of a morphologically derived rising tone is stressed (in Takum the end); 'The phonemic status of stress, here and elsewhere, has not been completely investigated. However, there is no evidence that it is phonemic, and in at least some phrases there appears to be some freedom in the position of stress.' No rule for a fixed stress position is given anywhere (full scanned grepped).

sources.note: Ch. I 'A System for Writing Wapan' (ms pp. 2-15) read page by page and scanned-grepped: CV syllable, palatalization/lip-rounding, nasal syllables, three tones H/M/L with derived fall and rise, tone always marked. The words 'stress'/'accent' never occur; 'emphasis' is used only for the post-verbal high-tone focus construction. Silent on word stress.

sources.citation: Anon. [Welmers/Dykstra papers] n.d. Phonological hierarchy of Jukun, Takum dialect. Unpublished typescript, 10 pp., Koeln Jukun-Manuskripte collection. [Takum = Diyi/Jukun Takum, jbu/juku1254, sister variety, not Wapan]
sources.note: Word-level demarcative features listed are initial nasal clusters, restricted consonant distribution and gliding tones confined to the word-final syllable; sentence question type marked by final-syllable lengthening; no mention of stress. Different glottocode (jbu); kept for reference only.

Need to confirm which variety it describes (Glottolog files it under Jukun Takum [jbu]; the Koeln Jukun page cites it for Wapan/Wukari).
